events.message: Mapped 23 files; 7 on the endpoint's code path
POST /inventory/reserve throughput_rps 187 req/s (goal: throughput of at least 240 req/s)
H1: Global asyncio.Lock serializes all reservations across SKUs

hypothesis.title: Global asyncio.Lock serializes all reservations across SKUs
hypothesis.explanation: The single `_inventory_lock` in inventory.py is acquired before any DB work and held for the entire transaction (SELECT, UPDATE, INSERT, INSERT). With 500 concurrent users and ~670ms latency, Little's Law gives ~125 in-flight requests. If the lock truly serialized the critical section, utilization would be >>1 and latency would explode. The stable 670ms latency suggests the lock is NOT the bottleneck, OR the critical section is much shorter than 670ms. The telemetry spans `inventory.lock_wait` and `inventory.lock_held` will reveal whether wait time dominates (lock contention) or held time dominates (slow critical section).
supporting_evidence: Code shows single global asyncio.Lock for all SKUs
contradicting_evidence: If lock serialized 670ms critical section, max throughput would be ~1.5 req/s, not 187

proposed_experiment.rationale: At low concurrency (100 users), lock contention should be minimal if the lock is the bottleneck at 500 users. If H1 is true, lock_wait will be near zero and lock_held will equal total latency (~670ms). If H1 is false (lock not the bottleneck), lock_wait will be near zero but lock_held will be much shorter than total latency, implicating other spans.

predictions.observation: inventory.lock_wait p50 < 20ms AND inventory.lock_held p50 ≈ 650-700ms
predictions.if_supported: Lock is held for nearly the entire request duration; at 500 users the queue would be massive but latency is stable, so this would be paradoxical and suggest measurement artifact.
predictions.if_refuted: Lock is not the primary latency contributor; bottleneck lies in DB operations or elsewhere.

predictions.observation: inventory.lock_wait p50 < 20ms AND inventory.lock_held p50 < 100ms
predictions.if_supported: Critical section is fast; total latency comes from other spans (DB round-trips, pool acquire, etc.). Lock contention is low even at 500 users.
predictions.if_refuted: Lock wait is significant even at 100 users, indicating lock pathology (e.g., lock held across await points causing convoy effect).

events.message: H2: Database transaction latency (4 round-trips in single transaction) dominates response time

hypothesis.title: Database transaction latency (4 round-trips in single transaction) dominates response time
hypothesis.explanation: The `_reserve_locked` function performs 4 sequential await points inside one transaction: pool_acquire, fetchrow (SELECT), execute (UPDATE), fetchval (INSERT reservation), execute (INSERT inventory_event). Each round-trip to Postgres adds latency. With local DB, each may take 1-2ms, but asyncpg driver overhead, transaction management, and connection pooling could inflate this. The telemetry spans `db.pool_acquire`, `db.select_stock`, `db.update_stock`, `db.insert_reservation`, `db.insert_inventory_event` will show which step dominates.
supporting_evidence: Code shows 4 await points in critical section
DB CPU low (11-13%) suggests I/O wait, not CPU
No indexes on products.sku beyond PK (but PK is sku, so SELECT is indexed)
contradicting_evidence: 4 local DB round-trips should take <10ms total, not 670ms

proposed_experiment.rationale: If DB round-trips dominate, the sum of DB spans will equal total latency. If not, the gap implicates lock wait, pool wait, or driver overhead.

predictions.observation: Sum of db.* spans p50 ≈ 650-700ms (matching HTTP p50)
predictions.if_supported: Database transaction is the bottleneck. Individual spans will show which operation (pool_acquire, select, update, inserts) is slowest.
predictions.if_refuted: Database is fast; bottleneck is elsewhere (lock, event loop, driver).

predictions.observation: db.pool_acquire p50 > 100ms
predictions.if_supported: Connection pool exhaustion (max 20) even at 100 users, because lock serializes pool acquisition.
predictions.if_refuted: Pool acquisition is fast; pool size not a factor.

events.message: H3: asyncpg driver / event-loop overhead inflates latency per await point

hypothesis.title: asyncpg driver / event-loop overhead inflates latency per await point
hypothesis.explanation: Each `await` on asyncpg methods (fetchrow, execute, fetchval) yields control to the event loop. With 125 concurrent requests, the event loop processes many ready callbacks per I/O completion. The telemetry uses `time.perf_counter()` which measures wall time including scheduler delays. If the event loop is saturated, each await adds scheduling latency. The `http POST /inventory/reserve` span minus sum of all child spans would reveal 'missing time' attributable to event-loop scheduling.
supporting_evidence: 125 concurrent coroutines all yielding at DB await points
Telemetry spans use perf_counter (includes scheduler delay)
contradicting_evidence: App CPU only 34-38% suggests event loop not saturated
asyncio typically handles thousands of concurrent I/O waits easily
missing_evidence: Gap between HTTP span and sum of child spans
Event loop lag metrics (not directly instrumented)

proposed_experiment.rationale: If event-loop scheduling adds significant latency, the HTTP span will exceed the sum of all instrumented child spans by a large margin. At 100 users, this gap should be smaller if it scales with concurrency.

predictions.observation: HTTP span p50 - sum(child spans p50) > 200ms at 500 users, but < 50ms at 100 users
predictions.if_supported: Event-loop scheduling delay scales with concurrency. The 'missing time' is the bottleneck.
predictions.if_refuted: Gap is small at both levels; latency is fully accounted by instrumented spans.

predictions.if_supported: Lock convoy effect: many waiters, each holder yields at await, causing thundering herd on lock release.
predictions.if_refuted: Lock wait grows linearly or stays flat; no convoy effect.

events.message: H4: Global asyncio.Lock serializes all reservations across SKUs, causing queueing delay that dominates latency at high concurrency

hypothesis.title: Global asyncio.Lock serializes all reservations across SKUs, causing queueing delay that dominates latency at high concurrency
hypothesis.explanation: The lab notebook marks H1 as 'DISPROVED (95%)' but the evidence actually confirms it: at 500 concurrent users, inventory.lock_wait p50 = 490.1 ms (p99 595.5 ms) across 4146 calls, while inventory.lock_held p50 = only 4.7 ms. HTTP POST /inventory/reserve p50 = 495.0 ms, meaning ~99% of request latency is spent waiting for the global lock. The lock is held for ~4.7 ms (db.transaction p50 = 4.1 ms), so with 500 concurrent users the queueing delay dominates. This global lock prevents concurrent reservations for different SKUs, which the database could handle natively via row-level locking (SELECT FOR UPDATE).
supporting_evidence: At 500 users: lock_wait p50=490.1 ms (4146 calls), lock_held p50=4.7 ms (4147 calls), HTTP p50=495.0 ms (4147 calls)
At 100 users: lock_wait p50=0.0 ms, lock_held p50=4.8 ms, HTTP p50=5.3 ms — lock contention only appears under high concurrency
db.transaction p50=4.1 ms (p99 5.2 ms) at 100 users, confirming the critical section is short
Sum of DB operation spans (select_stock 0.7 ms + update_stock 0.7 ms + insert_reservation 0.7 ms + insert_inventory_event 0.7 ms) ≈ 2.8 ms p50, far below 670 ms baseline latency
missing_evidence: Direct measurement of throughput with the global lock removed (to confirm 240+ req/s is achievable)

proposed_experiment.rationale: Remove the global asyncio.Lock and replace it with SELECT FOR UPDATE in the database transaction to serialize only conflicting SKUs. This should eliminate the lock_wait queueing delay and allow parallel reservations for different SKUs, increasing throughput from ~187 to >240 req/s.

key_observations: At 500 concurrent users, inventory.lock_wait p50 = 527.9 ms (p99 636.7 ms) across 4099 calls, while inventory.lock_held p50 = 4.8 ms (p99 6.8 ms). HTTP POST /inventory/reserve p50 = 532.9 ms, meaning ~99% of request latency (527.9/532.9) is spent waiting for the global lock.
lock_held (4.8 ms p50) closely matches db.transaction (4.1 ms p50), confirming the lock is held only for the actual database work (~4 ms), not for the entire request latency.

At 100 concurrent users, lock_wait p50 = 0.0 ms (p99 10.7 ms) and HTTP p50 = 5.4 ms, showing the queueing delay only dominates at high concurrency where 500 users contend for a ~4 ms critical section.
Throughput at 500 users is 197.0 req/s, consistent with Little's Law: 500 users / (0.533 s + 2 s think) ≈ 197 req/s, confirming the lock queueing delay is the throughput limiter.

db.transaction p50 remains 4.1 ms (unchanged from prior runs), and individual DB operation spans (select_stock, update_stock, insert_reservation, insert_inventory_event) are all sub-millisecond, confirming database work is not the bottleneck.
conclusion.explanation: The experiment measured the unmodified code (global asyncio.Lock still present). The measurements confirm H4: at 500 concurrent users, the global lock serializes all reservations across SKUs, causing a queueing delay (lock_wait p50 = 527.9 ms) that dominates the 532.9 ms HTTP latency. The lock is held for only ~4.8 ms (the actual DB transaction), so with 500 users the queueing delay grows super-linearly and limits throughput to ~197 req/s. The hypothesis that the global lock is the bottleneck is strongly supported by the current-code measurements. The predictions about post-fix behavior could not be tested because the fix was not applied; this conclusion evaluates the hypothesis against the current system state.

candidate.name: per-sku-locking
candidate.strategy: Replace the global asyncio.Lock with a per-SKU lock dictionary (defaultdict), allowing concurrent reservations for different SKUs while still serializing access to the same SKU.
candidate.expected_effect: Eliminates cross-SKU contention. At 500 concurrent users with uniform SKU distribution, lock_wait p50 should drop from ~528 ms to near 0 ms (only same-SKU collisions queue). HTTP p50 should fall from ~533 ms to ~5 ms (db.transaction p50). Throughput should scale linearly with concurrency, exceeding 240 req/s at 500 users.
candidate.risks: Memory grows with number of SKUs accessed (1000 SKUs = 1000 locks, negligible). If workload concentrates on few hot SKUs, those SKUs still serialize but no worse than global lock. Lock dictionary access is synchronous and yield-free, safe in asyncio. Must ensure locks are released in finally block (already done).

events.message: database-row-locking: Remove the application-level asyncio.Lock entirely and rely on PostgreSQL's row-level locking via SELECT ... FOR UPDATE. The database natively serializes concurrent updates to the same product row while allowing full concurrency across different SKUs.

candidate.name: database-row-locking
candidate.strategy: Remove the application-level asyncio.Lock entirely and rely on PostgreSQL's row-level locking via SELECT ... FOR UPDATE. The database natively serializes concurrent updates to the same product row while allowing full concurrency across different SKUs.
candidate.expected_effect: Eliminates application-level queueing entirely. At 500 concurrent users, lock_wait spans disappear. HTTP p50 should match db.transaction p50 (~4 ms). Throughput at 500 users should exceed 240 req/s (Little's Law: 500 / (0.004 + 2) ≈ 249 req/s). Database handles contention via row locks, which are held only for the ~4 ms transaction.
candidate.risks: Relies on PostgreSQL's MVCC and row locking correctness (battle-tested). Long-running transactions could increase lock hold time, but current transaction is ~4 ms p50. Must ensure SELECT FOR UPDATE is placed inside the transaction (it is). No application-level lock state to leak or deadlock. Slightly higher database lock contention on hot SKUs vs per-SKU lock, but database lock is more granular (row vs application critical section).

events.message: optimistic-concurrency-control: Remove the application-level lock and use optimistic locking: read stock, then UPDATE with a WHERE clause that checks stock hasn't changed (WHERE sku = $1 AND stock = $2). On conflict (0 rows updated), retry up to a small fixed number of times with a brief delay. This avoids both application locks and long database row locks.

candidate.name: optimistic-concurrency-control
candidate.strategy: Remove the application-level lock and use optimistic locking: read stock, then UPDATE with a WHERE clause that checks stock hasn't changed (WHERE sku = $1 AND stock = $2). On conflict (0 rows updated), retry up to a small fixed number of times with a brief delay. This avoids both application locks and long database row locks.
candidate.expected_effect: Eliminates application-level queueing. At low contention, zero retries; at high contention, brief retries (5 ms each) replace multi-second lock waits. HTTP p50 at 500 users should be ~10-20 ms (db work + occasional retry). Throughput should exceed 240 req/s. Retries are rare because the critical section is ~4 ms; conflict probability scales with (concurrency * critical_section / think_time).
candidate.risks: Under extreme contention on a single SKU, retries may exhaust and return 409 (InsufficientStock) even if stock exists, slightly reducing success rate. Mitigated by 5 retries and 5 ms delay (conflict window ~4 ms). Must parse asyncpg's "UPDATE n" result string correctly. Adds a new exception path (ConcurrencyConflict) but converts to InsufficientStock with re-read stock to preserve API behavior. Telemetry spans inside retry loop may record multiple db.transaction spans per request; this is acceptable.

candidates.name: optimistic-concurrency-control
candidates.strategy: Remove the application-level lock and use optimistic locking: read stock, then UPDATE with a WHERE clause that checks stock hasn't changed (WHERE sku = $1 AND stock = $2). On conflict (0 rows updated), retry up to a small fixed number of times with a brief delay. This avoids both application locks and long database row locks.
candidates.expected_effect: Eliminates application-level queueing. At low contention, zero retries; at high contention, brief retries (5 ms each) replace multi-second lock waits. HTTP p50 at 500 users should be ~10-20 ms (db work + occasional retry). Throughput should exceed 240 req/s. Retries are rare because the critical section is ~4 ms; conflict probability scales with (concurrency * critical_section / think_time).
candidates.risks: Under extreme contention on a single SKU, retries may exhaust and return 409 (InsufficientStock) even if stock exists, slightly reducing success rate. Mitigated by 5 retries and 5 ms delay (conflict window ~4 ms). Must parse asyncpg's "UPDATE n" result string correctly. Adds a new exception path (ConcurrencyConflict) but converts to InsufficientStock with re-read stock to preserve API behavior. Telemetry spans inside retry loop may record multiple db.transaction spans per request; this is acceptable.
